issues.legal_issue: A tenant must receive leave to contest a summary eviction application when the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that, if established at trial, would defeat the landlord’s claim.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession on the ground of bona fide residential need and asserted that no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation was available.
The tenant’s affidavit disputed the purpose for which the premises had been let and alleged that the landlord had other suitable accommodation and had repeatedly let out comparable vacant premises.
The Controller refused leave after deciding disputed factual matters on the affidavits as though they were evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Controller had to grant leave because the tenant disclosed facts which, if believed at trial, could disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 14(1)(e) and 25B(4)–(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, the landlord bears the burden of establishing the statutory grounds for eviction, and the Controller must grant leave if the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that could defeat the claim. The statutory wording requires disclosure, not proof, and differs from the substantial-defence language of Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court relied on Santosh Kumar v. Bhai Mool Singh and approved S. Kanjibhai v. Mohanraj Rajendra Kumar and Kishan Singh v. Mohd. Shafi. It also stressed that rent restriction legislation must not be interpreted so as to make tenant protections illusory, referring to Bahadur Singh v. Muni Sabrat Das, Kaushalya Devi v. R.L. Bansal and Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Rehman.

predicates.summary_residential_need_eviction_procee: A landlord has brought a summary eviction proceeding based on a claimed bona fide need for residential occupation.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_that_if: The tenant has stated in an affidavit facts which, if established at trial, could defeat the landlord’s claim to possession.
predicates.leave_to_contest_must_be_granted: The tenant is allowed to contest the eviction application.

issues.definition: When a summary residential-need eviction proceeding is brought and the tenant’s affidavit states facts that could defeat the landlord’s claim if established, the tenant must be allowed to contest the application.

issues.legal_issue: At the leave-to-contest stage, the Controller must assess whether the tenant has disclosed potentially decisive facts and must not determine disputed facts by weighing untested affidavits or documents.
material_facts: The tenant alleged that the landlord had suitable alternative accommodation and had let comparable premises to successive occupants, including at increased rents.
The landlord disputed those allegations in a reply affidavit and referred to other material.
The Controller treated the competing affidavits as evidence, resolved factual disputes and refused leave without a trial.
issues.conclusion: The Controller exceeded the permitted scope of inquiry by deciding disputed facts at the leave stage; the inquiry was limited to the tenant’s affidavit and any reply, and whether the disclosed facts could defeat the claim if later proved.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 25B(4)–(7) distinguish the leave stage from the later trial: at the leave stage the Controller considers disclosure, while, after leave is granted, the proceeding is heard under the prescribed trial procedure. The landlord may controvert the tenant’s affidavit by a reply, but proof or disproof through evidence or documents is not to be undertaken at that stage. The Court relied on Santosh Kumar v. Bhai Mool Singh and the procedural principles in Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah and Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India.

predicates.summary_eviction_leave_proceeding: A tenant has sought leave to contest a summary eviction application before the proceeding has reached trial.
predicates.controller_resolves_disputed_facts_by_we: The Controller decides contested factual matters by weighing affidavits or documents that have not been tested or proved at trial.
predicates.fact_finding_at_leave_stage_is_impermiss: The Controller may not resolve disputed facts by weighing untested material at the leave stage.

issues.definition: In a summary eviction leave proceeding, the Controller may not decide disputed facts by weighing untested material before trial.

issues.legal_issue: The general procedural requirements in section 37(1) do not require the Controller to receive evidence when deciding whether to grant leave to contest under the special summary procedure.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest an eviction application governed by the special procedure for claims of residential need.
It was argued that the Controller had to consider evidence under the general procedural provision while deciding the leave application.
issues.conclusion: Section 37(1) did not apply at the leave stage; the special procedure governed, and the general procedure became applicable after leave was granted.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 25B(1), 25B(7) and 25B(10) establish a self-contained procedure for the relevant eviction applications. Section 25B(7) specifies the procedure for the inquiry under that chapter, and section 25B(10) brings in the ordinary procedure for disposal after leave is granted. Applying section 37(1) at the leave stage would make those provisions redundant.

predicates.summary_eviction_leave_proceeding: A tenant has sought leave to contest an eviction application governed by a special summary procedure.
predicates.controller_is_deciding_whether_to_grant_: The Controller is deciding whether the tenant may contest before the substantive eviction hearing.
predicates.general_evidence_procedure_does_not_appl: The general procedure requiring consideration of evidence does not govern the decision on leave.

issues.definition: When the Controller is deciding whether to grant leave in a summary eviction proceeding, the general evidence procedure does not govern that decision.

issues.legal_issue: The leave standard for a summary residential-need eviction proceeding cannot be narrowed by importing the substantial-defence test applicable to summary suits under the Code of Civil Procedure.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest a summary eviction application based on residential need.
The parties relied on authorities comparing the leave provision with the procedure for summary suits under the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: The summary-suit test did not limit the Controller’s duty: disclosure of potentially decisive facts was sufficient, and the comparison could not narrow the statutory power and duty to grant leave.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25B(5) uses mandatory language and requires leave when the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession. Order XXXVII, rule 3(5) uses a different test and permits conditional or issue-limited leave, powers not conferred on the Controller by section 25B(5). The Court considered Busching Schmitz (P) Ltd. v. P.T. Menghani, B.N. Mutta v. T.R. Nandi, Charan Dass Duggal v. Brahma Nand and Om Prakash Saluja v. Saraswati Devi, and disapproved the contrary interpretation in Mohanlal v. Tirath Ram Chopra.

predicates.summary_residential_need_eviction_procee: A landlord has brought a summary eviction proceeding based on a claimed bona fide need for residential occupation.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_potentially_d: The tenant’s affidavit states facts which, if established, could defeat the landlord’s claim.
predicates.disclosure_not_substantial_defence_is_th: The Controller applies the disclosure standard rather than requiring the tenant to establish a substantial defence at the leave stage.

issues.definition: In a summary residential-need eviction proceeding, the Controller uses disclosure of potentially decisive facts, not a substantial-defence requirement, to decide whether to grant leave.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant must receive leave to contest when the affidavit raises substantial disputes about the landlord’s bona fide need and alternative accommodation that require a trial.
material_facts: The landlord had returned and settled in the city but had renewed the tenant’s leave-and-licence arrangement after returning.

The tenant alleged that an identical unit behind the premises had become vacant and had been let to successive tenants, and the landlord acknowledged that the unit was occupied by another tenant until a later period.
The tenant alleged that the landlord had other suitable accommodation and had repeatedly let vacant premises at higher rents.
Although an eviction notice had been served, the landlord did not pursue the claim for several years before serving a further notice.
The landlord did not provide sworn details of his residential requirements or the basis on which he occupied the accommodation where he was then living.
The Controller resolved the disputed allegations on the affidavits and refused leave; the High Court dismissed the revision.
issues.conclusion: The disclosed facts put the landlord’s bona fides and the availability of suitable alternative accommodation in issue. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the orders refusing leave and granted the tenant leave to contest, remitting the case for proceedings according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 25B(5), allegations concerning alternative accommodation, repeated reletting of comparable premises, conduct bearing on bona fide need, and the landlord’s failure to explain his existing accommodation may disclose facts which, if proved, would defeat a residential-need eviction claim. The Controller must not decide those disputed matters at the leave stage. The Court applied its construction of sections 14(1)(e) and 25B(4)–(5), and the principles in Santosh Kumar v. Bhai Mool Singh and Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah.
